help.updates_the_updates_row: The Updates row in Settings › System › Status shows this version and whether a newer one is out. Check for updates looks now; it also looks every 12 hours ([update] check = false in the config stops that). Nothing is installed until an admin clicks Update and confirms. An update stops AmberSight for about a minute (no recording, no live view; longer on big sites), and playback and the timeline can be slow for a few minutes after the restart while it checks its recordings (a small notice says so). If the update changes the database, a copy is saved first in the backups folder (pre-upgrade-...; on a big database on a spinning drive this can add a minute or more before recording starts again), and going back to the older version afterwards is not recommended: it runs, but warns, and ignores the newer parts. AmberSight then downloads the package for this computer, checks it is signed by the AmberSight release key (an unsigned or changed package is refused), keeps the current program in the previous folder next to it, and restarts when it runs as a service (otherwise restart it yourself). To go back, stop AmberSight and copy the files from previous over the program. Installed with apt or dnf (a .deb or .rpm package)? Update with apt or dnf instead. From a terminal: ambersight update --config config.toml (--check only looks; it asks before installing, --yes skips the question). Updates with apt, dnf or the Windows installer cannot ask first, but have the same effects.
help.your_account_a_qr_code: A QR code for phone sign-in from the Users page still works for an account with two-step codes: the admin who made it vouches for that person. Making an admin, setting someone else's password, turning off someone's codes, a QR code for an admin or an account with two-step codes, enabling a disabled admin, commands that run programs (external detector, alert action), where backups go, linking servers, and where or whether alerts arrive all take the admin's own password (and code), so a stolen session alone cannot do them. That last one means the alert services, the address notifications open, system alerts and how soon they go out, the Pushover sound, taking a push server off the list, turning off or narrowing the morning summary, and turning on the watchdog or letting it wait or try longer (it holds back the offline alert while it works). A session that keeps getting that wrong is signed out and admins are told. Admins also hear when an admin adds or removes a device for notifications, and when a restart is asked for. New usernames are at most 64 characters, with nothing that does not show. Sign-in from a linked server does not: that person signs in here with their code.
help.your_account_device_tokens_are: Device tokens are for programs that watch or do everyday things and cannot ask for a code, such as Home Assistant or an RTSP player. Make one in Your account, give it a name, and copy it: it is shown only once. A watch-only token sees live video, events, clips and recordings. One with day-to-day control can also arm and disarm, change profile and pause notifications (for a day at most), move cameras, record a clip and review events; admins are told when it disarms or pauses. It cannot save presets or start tours. No token can change settings, passwords or accounts, get notifications, or report presence: an app that needs those signs in with a password or a QR code. Each works until you revoke it, also after you change your password. An admin who stops being an admin loses tokens with control for good.
help.your_account_lost_your_phone: Lost your phone? Use a recovery code on the sign-in page. No codes left? Another admin can turn it off for you in Users (Edit). If you are the only admin, someone with access to the computer can run ambersight user reset-two-step <name> --config <file>, and if the password may be known, ambersight user set-password <name> --config <file>.
help.your_account_new_device_alerts: New device alerts. When an account signs in from a browser it has not used before, admins get one message that names the account, the device, the address and how (password, two-step code, recovery code, QR code, a linked server, or a password sent directly by a program). Several in a minute are joined into one more message. Each browser is recognized by a small cookie, kept up to two years, that gives no access by itself (a program that signs in on every run should keep that cookie too, or use a device token, or admins are told every time). Nothing is sent for a first sign-in to a new account, or when the same browser already has a working session; after an update each browser is told once, the next time it signs in without one. A program that sends the password directly (HTTP Basic or RTSP) is told once per account and network, and its message says to change the password. Changing a password forgets every known browser except the one you changed it from, so each of your other browsers is told once at its next sign-in. Changing a password also signs the other devices out, and takes off the notifications they had turned on, so a device that is still signed in keeps getting alerts but one that was signed out does not until you sign in on it again (the page turns its notifications back on at sign-in). The phone of an admin that loses alerts this way, or by Sign out in Your account, is told, and the admins are told too. A second sign-in of the browser you are using is not forgotten. A plain Sign out keeps the browser known. These messages go out even when Alert when something is wrong is off.
help.your_account_nobody_has_to: Nobody has to use them, but we recommend them for admin accounts.
help.your_account_rtsp_is_not: RTSP is not encrypted, so it takes watch-only tokens only: your username with the token as the password. Use it on a network you trust.
help.your_account_signed_in_devices: Signed-in devices. Your account lists every browser and phone that is signed in to it: its kind (such as Edge on Windows), the address it last came from, when it signed in and when it was last used. Sign out one you do not recognize with Sign out, or all but this one with Sign out all other devices. A device signed out here is signed out at once, and any video it had open ends. No password is asked for; if one is not yours, change your password too. Signing a device out also makes its browser new again, and takes off the notifications it turned on (ones turned on before this list existed cannot be matched: remove older devices in the account menu under Notifications on this device). Video open on your other devices stops for a moment and reconnects. Devices that signed in before this list existed show as Signed in before this list existed and keep working. Device tokens are listed separately below.
help.your_account_someone_keeps_entering: Someone keeps entering wrong codes? Then they have your password. Admins get a warning. Change the password right away: a device that is still signed in can do it with your code, whatever is locked at the sign-in page. An address with too many wrong codes waits 10 minutes; other addresses are not affected, unless there are very many tries. A recovery code always works at the sign-in page, also during such a wait.
help.your_account_two_step_codes: Two-step codes mean a stolen password alone does not get anyone in. Open the menu at the top, Your account, and turn them on: scan the picture with an authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Aegis and others), then type the code it shows. Save the 10 recovery codes somewhere that is not your phone: each one signs you in once if the phone is lost.
help.your_account_your_own_password: Your own password. Always takes your current password, and your code when two-step codes are on. An admin who disabled the wrong account, or is locked out, can run ambersight user enable <name> --config <file> on the computer.

settings.hw_hint: Auto tries an NVIDIA card first, then Intel Quick Sync (VAAPI on older Intel chips), then VAAPI on Intel or AMD, and uses the processor when none works. A camera with its own Hardware decoding setting keeps it. A change applies within seconds, without a restart.
settings.hw_keep_free: Keep free on the NVIDIA card
settings.hw_lead: Where motion detection decodes the picture: on a graphics card, or on the processor.
settings.hw_min_free_desc: Auto and Prefer Intel / AMD put a camera on the NVIDIA card only while this much video memory stays free after it (a decoder takes about 300 MB), so the AI and other programs on the card keep room. Cameras that did not fit use Intel or the processor and move back when there is 1 GB more. 0 turns the check off. Prefer NVIDIA and a camera's own NVIDIA setting ignore it.
settings.hw_no_card: No graphics card that can decode was found: motion detection decodes on the processor.
settings.hw_none: No camera is decoding right now.
settings.hw_nvidia_mem: NVIDIA card memory: {used} of {total} GB used ({free} GB free). {keep}
settings.hw_nvidia_missing: NVIDIA card memory: nvidia-smi was not found, so Auto does not check for free memory.
settings.hw_test_desc1: At start, each way (NVIDIA NVDEC, Intel Quick Sync, VAAPI) decodes a short H.264 and H.265 sample and its pictures are compared with the processor's; a way that fails is never used by Auto.
settings.hw_test_desc2: Prefer NVIDIA puts the NVIDIA card first with no memory check. Prefer Intel / AMD puts it last.
settings.hw_test_desc3: When a way fails while running, that camera moves to the next way, or the processor, at once, and tries the failed way again after 15 minutes, then after longer waits (up to 4 hours). A second failure in a row (with no 30 minutes of good running between) makes it leave that way until AmberSight restarts or a setting on this page changes. The NVIDIA card running out of memory is only waited out.
settings.hw_test_desc4: A camera keeps its place on the NVIDIA card through a short reconnect and gives it up after about 2 minutes offline.
settings.hw_test_desc5: Linux: Quick Sync on Intel Gen12 and newer needs Intel's GPU runtime (sudo apt install libmfx-gen1.2 on Debian and Ubuntu, intel-vpl-gpu-rt on Fedora; then restart AmberSight). Windows: an NVIDIA card that passed the test, otherwise the processor. macOS: the processor.
settings.hw_test_desc6: In the config: [hwdecode] prefer = "auto" (or nvidia, intel, off) and nvidia_min_free_mb = 1536.
settings.hw_test_running: The start-up test of the graphics cards is still running.

Everything it does is listed in Settings, System, Audit. It never acts in the first 5 minutes after AmberSight starts, at most once an hour per camera, and not at all while most cameras are offline at once (that is the network or the power, not the cameras). Disabled, sleeping battery and other servers' cameras are left alone.

share_settings.how: Other apps connect here instead of to each camera, so the cameras only ever serve AmberSight. The video is passed on as it arrives (no re-encoding, almost no extra load), with sound when the camera has AAC audio. Off until you turn it on, and only for the cameras you switch on below. Apps sign in with an AmberSight account (user name and password, sent as HTTP Basic); accounts limited to some cameras only see those.
share_settings.how_use_addresses_body: Home Assistant: Settings, Devices & services, Add integration, Generic Camera. Stream source: the main or sub stream address, with USER and PASSWORD filled in (a password with special characters must be percent-encoded, @ is %40). RTSP transport protocol: TCP. Still image URL: the Snapshot address, with the same user name and password in the authentication fields (basic); the MJPEG address works as a stream source too. If this server uses HTTPS with its own certificate, turn off certificate verification there.

share_settings.tcp_hint: Only TCP is offered (UDP is not). Shared video is the camera's own picture, without AmberSight's drawn text. The camera sound is shared when it is AAC; G.711 sound is not (video only).
share_settings.vlc_hint: VLC: Media, Open Network Stream, paste the address (it asks for the user name and password if they are not in it). Another NVR: add a generic RTSP camera with the address; choose TCP.
